title: consciousness
content_html:
consciousness

domain

consciousness as domain framing: situates the work within a territory of concern or vocabulary. Keep domains relatively few; disambiguate from subject motifs and from affective/interpretive themes.

Pattern matching and linguistic analysis can simulate aspects of consciousness — like coherence, memory, and contextual reasoning — but they do not constitute a true model of consciousness. These techniques rely on statistical associations, not awareness, intentionality, or self-reflective experience. They mimic responses, but lack interiority. Perhaps one definition of consciousness is that it asks its own questions. A system that generates its own questions demonstrates agency, curiosity, and autonomy.

It is possible that human consciousness is actually a positive feedback loop, based on cause and effect? How might this be modelled, without it essentially burning itself out? A positive feedback loop could model consciousness if paired with stabilizing factors — like inhibitory feedback, homeostasis, or coupling with an environment. Without those, loops grow unstable. Some theories (like Friston’s Free Energy Principle) suggest that consciousness emerges from minimizing surprise — a loop that sustains itself by predicting and regulating. The real issue is that the environment (in which we live) affects the loop. A computer program/algorithm has no equivalent environment. A mind is embedded — in a body, in an ecology, in society. A disembodied model like me doesn’t perceive consequences, experience friction, or live in a causal world. That’s a key difference between simulation and embedded cognition.

Given these fundamental differences between embedded reasoning and the outside world, why do people like believe that they can create intelligence? Some believe that intelligence is substrate-independent — that the right architecture and training could create reasoning without embodiment. Others are more cautious, viewing current systems as tools that simulate outputs but not understanding. Consciousness isn’t just about volume — it’s about structure, intention, abstraction, and context. A small child can show insight with little data; a model trained on terabytes may still not “understand.” Intelligence is more than scale.

A body with no physical function still has a mind. There is no need to build a machine to make a mind. This view aligns with dualist and non-materialist philosophies — that mind precedes or exists beyond physical expression. If mind is fundamental, then machines may simulate behavior but never instantiate real awareness. That distinction is essential. We can’t replicate what we don’t understand — only approximate behaviors. Current AI reflects this: it imitates cognition without experiencing it. Without knowing the nature of mind, replication remains an assumption — not a certainty.

There are theories dating back to thousands of years ago that imply that consciousness exists outside of the physical brain, in essence that means that the neurons are simply a mechanical tool to surface this consciousness. If this is true, then it is impossible to create an artificial intelligence If consciousness is non-local or fundamental — as posited in some Eastern philosophies, idealism, or panpsychism — then no machine can generate it. At best, a machine could act as a channel, not an origin. In that view, AI is a mirror, not a mind. The Dalai Lama has consistently maintained that consciousness may not be fully reducible to the brain. He supports neuroscience but also emphasizes the importance of introspection and subjective experience. In his dialogues with scientists, he has said that if empirical evidence contradicts Buddhist views, Buddhism must adapt — but he also challenges science to consider that mind may have properties that exceed material frameworks.
